claims.text: Catalytic activity in transition-metal hydrogenation catalysts is governed by the density of coordinatively unsaturated surface sites.
Hydrogenation selectivity is governed by the density of coordinatively unsaturated surface sites.
Reduction pretreatment forms coordinatively unsaturated surface sites.
Coordinatively unsaturated sites enhance adsorption and activation of molecular hydrogen.
Coordinatively unsaturated sites enhance adsorption and activation of substrate molecules.
The as-synthesized catalyst has a relatively oxidized or non-optimized surface structure.
Hydrogen reduction pretreatment induces surface reconstruction.
Reduction-induced reconstruction exposes more low-coordinated metal atoms.
Low-coordinated metal atoms have electronic properties favorable for hydrogen activation and reactant adsorption.
The proposed changes in adsorption and hydrogen activation lower the activation energy of hydrogenation.
Reduction-pretreated catalysts will have higher turnover frequencies than untreated catalysts.
Reduction-pretreated catalysts will have greater selectivity for the desired hydrogenation product than untreated catalysts.
Catalytic performance will correlate with the measured density of coordinatively unsaturated surface sites.
The proposed relationship should hold for transition-metal catalysts that reconstruct under reducing conditions and for reactions sensitive to metal coordination and electronic structure.
Very high temperatures that cause sintering can prevent the proposed trend from holding.
Strongly oxidizing conditions can prevent the proposed trend from holding.
